warmup.q: A log helper reads when (event) { is PaymentCaptured -> "capture"; is PaymentRefunded -> "refund"; else -> "other" }. A teammate adds PaymentDisputed to the sealed PaymentEvent interface and ships. What happens to disputes?
options: The build fails until the helper handles PaymentDisputed
They are logged as "other", and nothing tells anyone
The helper throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException at run time
Kotlin adds a branch for the new type automatically
warmup.why: The else branch matches anything, including types that didn't exist when it was written, so the compiler has nothing to report. Without the else, the same change is a compile error at this exact line. NoWhenBranchMatchedException only appears when a subtype compiled later reaches a when that was exhaustive when it was compiled.

sections.h: What you'll build, and why it starts with the model
sections.html:
Over three lessons you'll build one small library: an in-process event library for a payments service. This lesson is the model, the types for every event the service can see. Lesson 2 of this track is the bus that routes those events to handlers. Lesson 3 is the API that Kotlin and Java code call. Each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any lesson.

Start with what goes wrong without a model. The demo below has three handlers for messages from a Kafka topic, and each one reads the raw string fields itself:

Java
static void ledger(Map<String, String> fields) {
    if ("captured".equals(fields.get("type"))) {
        long cents = Long.parseLong(fields.get("amountMinor"));   // parsing, deep inside a handler
        balanceCents += cents;
    }
}
Kotlin
fun ledger(fields: Map<String, String>) {
    if (fields["type"] == "captured") {
        val cents = fields.getValue("amountMinor").toLong()      // parsing, deep inside a handler
        balanceCents += cents
    }
}

Two bugs come out of three messages. A capture with "amountMinor": "12.50" throws NumberFormatException inside the ledger, after the audit handler has already logged it as a capture. And the receipts handler compares the type with "capture", a typo, so it never fires and nothing complains. Each handler parses and checks for itself, so each one can get it wrong in its own way, and the compiler can't help with any of it.

The fix comes in three pieces, one per section. A closed set of event types, so the compiler knows every case; that's the tool from Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check. Small types for ids and amounts, so a bad value can't be built at all, from Value classes and what they compile to. And one function at the edge that turns raw fields into those types or refuses them, the idea from Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla. Behind that edge, no handler ever sees a string field again.

Before you run the demo, predict which message fails, in which handler, and how many receipts get sent.

The only place a check can stop pay_7782 before every handler is in front of all of them, which is the edge this lesson builds.

sections.h: A sealed interface lists every event the service can see
sections.html:
Here is the model. Every event is a fact about one payment, named in the past tense. A command asks for something; an event says it already happened, so handlers can't refuse it, only react.

Java
sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement {
    PaymentId paymentId();
}
record PaymentAuthorized(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements PaymentEvent {}
record PaymentDeclined(PaymentId paymentId, DeclineReason reason) implements PaymentEvent {}

sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded {
    Money amount();
}
record PaymentCaptured(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement {}
record PaymentRefunded(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement {}
Kotlin
sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: PaymentId }
data class PaymentAuthorized(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val amount: Money) : PaymentEvent
data class PaymentDeclined(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val reason: DeclineReason) : PaymentEvent

sealed interface MoneyMovement : PaymentEvent { val amount: Money }
data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement
data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement

sealed closes the list of direct subtypes. In Kotlin they must sit in the same package and the same module; Java lists them after permits. Data classes and records are final, so every branch ends at a leaf, except MoneyMovement, which is sealed again one level down. That middle level is a design decision you'll use in lesson 2: a handler for MoneyMovement will receive captures and refunds, and nothing else.

The payoff is the exhaustive when. Write it with no else, and the compiler checks that every leaf is covered:

Java
static boolean movesMoney(PaymentEvent e) {
    return switch (e) {
        case MoneyMovement m -> true;                 // one case covers both leaves
        case PaymentAuthorized a -> false;
        case PaymentDeclined d -> false;
    };
}
Kotlin
fun movesMoney(e: PaymentEvent): Boolean = when (e) {
    is MoneyMovement -> true                          // one branch covers both leaves
    is PaymentAuthorized, is PaymentDeclined -> false
}

Add a PaymentDisputed and every such when stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is PaymentDisputed' branch or an 'else' branch. As State and Chain of Responsibility put it, the compiler writes your to-do list. An else throws that list away: the new event quietly takes the else branch at every place nobody revisited.

One gap stays open at run time. If a jar compiled against the new model hands a PaymentDisputed to code compiled against the old one, Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException and Java throws MatchException. In this library events reach the service as raw fields and pass the edge first, so an old service rejects the unknown type there instead.

In the demo, uncomment PaymentDisputed and predict which of the three functions stop compiling.

sections.h: Value classes turn a swapped argument into a compile error
sections.html:
Look at this refund record: RawRefund("pay_7781", 30, 500). Is 30 the amount and 500 the fee, or the other way round? The constructor takes two Longs, so a swapped call compiles and moves the wrong money. Value classes make that a compile error:

Java
record PaymentId(String value) {
    PaymentId {
        if (!value.matches("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid payment id: '" + value + "'");
    }
}
record Money(long minor) {
    Money {
        if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative: " + minor);
    }
}
Kotlin
@JvmInline
value class PaymentId(val value: String) {
    init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid payment id: '$value'" } }
    override fun toString(): String = value
    companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}") }
}

@JvmInline
value class Money(val minor: Long) {
    init { require(minor >= 0) { "amount must not be negative: $minor" } }
    override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, 2).toPlainString()
}

Now PaymentCaptured(Money(1_999), PaymentId("pay_7781")) fails with argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Money', but 'PaymentId' was expected. And because init runs on every construction, a PaymentId that exists is a valid one. Nothing downstream needs to check the format again.

The cost is small, for the reason Value classes and what they compile to gave: where a value class is used as itself, the compiler erases it to its one field. The demo prints the fields of PaymentCaptured through Java reflection, and they are a java.lang.String and a long. The Java records are separate objects on the heap, one per id and one per amount. They are boxed in the places that lesson listed, such as a List<PaymentId>, a nullable Money? or a generic T.

The one-field rule also made a decision for this model. A real Money would carry its currency, but a value class can hold only one field until Project Valhalla arrives, and a data class with two fields would cost an object per amount. This service settles in euros only, so Money is euro cents and the currency lives nowhere. The design review in lesson 3 comes back to whether that was right.

Keep the explicit : String on Money.toString. When a value class's toString leaves out its return type and returns the result of a Java method such as toPlainString(), Kotlin 2.4.21 crashes with a backend error as soon as the value appears in a string template.

In the demo, uncomment the swapped constructor call and read both errors. Then compare the field types the Kotlin and Java versions print.

Kotlin's fields are java.lang.String and long; Java's are the nested PaymentId and Money record classes, each a separate object.

sections.h: Parse at the edge, then trust the types
sections.html:
The model refuses bad values, but bad values still arrive: from Kafka, from a webhook, from a database row someone edited by hand. So one function converts raw input into the model, in one place, at the edge of the service. It returns a result and never throws:

Java
static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) {
    try {
        String type = field(fields, "type");
        return switch (type) {
            case "captured" -> new Ok(new PaymentCaptured(new PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields)));
            // ... one case per type
            default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'");
        };
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return new Rejected(e.getMessage());     // a reader or a constructor said no
    }
}
Kotlin
fun parseEvent(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed = try {
    when (val type = field(fields, "type")) {
        "captured" -> Parsed.Ok(PaymentCaptured(PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields)))
        // ... one branch per type
        else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'")
    }
} catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
    Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event")  // a reader or a constructor said no
}

Notice what parse does not do: it doesn't check the payment id's format or the sign of the amount. It calls PaymentId(...) and Money(...) and turns their refusal into a Rejected. The rules live in the constructors, once. A second copy of them in the parser would drift the first time someone edits one and not the other.

Why a result instead of an exception? Because the caller has to decide what a bad message means, and an exception makes that decision for it. In a Kafka consumer, an exception that escapes the loop sends the consumer back to its last committed offset, so the same record fails again after every restart, and the partition behind it stops moving. A Rejected can go to a dead-letter topic with its reason as a header, add one to a metric and let the consumer commit the offset and move on. Never retry it: a malformed message stays malformed.

Behind the edge, code trusts the types. A function that takes a PaymentCaptured has a valid id and a positive amount, because no other kind of PaymentCaptured can exist. There is no !!, no toLong() and no if (type == ...) anywhere in the handlers you'll write in lesson 2.

The demo's parser knows only captures and refunds. Predict which of its six messages are rejected, and for what reason, before you run it.

try.title: Run six messages through the edge
steps: Read the six messages in EdgeDemo's main. For each, predict OK or REJECTED and the reason.
Run it.
Add a declined branch: a PaymentDeclined(paymentId, reason: String) data class (a record in Java), and a branch that reads the reason field. Run it again and check the count line.

code.title: EdgeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l01.demo.edge @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) { init { require(Regex("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}").matches(value)) { "invalid payment id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value } @JvmInline value class Money(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "amount must not be negative: $minor" } } override fun toString(): String = "$minor cents" } sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: PaymentId } data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val amount: Money) : PaymentEvent data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val amount: Money) : PaymentEvent sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val event: PaymentEvent) : Parsed data class Rejected(val reason: String) : Parsed } /** The edge: raw fields in, a model value or a reason out. It never throws. */ fun parse(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed { fun field(name: String) = fields[name] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("missing field '$name'") fun amount(): Money { val raw = field("amountMinor") return Money(raw.toLongOrNull() ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("amountMinor is not a whole number: '$raw'")) } return try { when (val type = field("type")) { "captured" -> Parsed.Ok(PaymentCaptured(PaymentId(field("paymentId")), amount())) "refunded" -> Parsed.Ok(PaymentRefunded(PaymentId(field("paymentId")), amount())) else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event") // a constructor or a reader said no } } fun main() { val inbox = listOf( mapOf("type" to "captured", "paymentId" to "pay_7781", "amountMinor" to "1999"), mapOf("type" to "captured", "paymentId" to "pay_7782", "amountMinor" to "12.50"), mapOf("type" to "refunded", "paymentId" to "7781", "amountMinor" to "500"), mapOf("type" to "refunded", "paymentId" to "pay_7781", "amountMinor" to "-500"), mapOf("type" to "captured", "paymentId" to "pay_7783"), mapOf("type" to "declined", "paymentId" to "pay_7784", "reason" to "CARD_EXPIRED"), ) var accepted = 0 for (fields in inbox) { when (val p = parse(fields)) { is Parsed.Ok -> { accepted++; println("OK ${p.event}") } is Parsed.Rejected -> println("REJECTED ${p.reason}") } } println("$accepted accepted, ${inbox.size - accepted} rejected") }

alt.title: EdgeDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l01.demo.edge; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; public class EdgeDemoJava { record PaymentId(String value) { PaymentId { if (!value.matches("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid payment id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Money(long minor) { Money { if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative: " + minor); } @Override public String toString() { return minor + " cents"; } } sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded {} record PaymentCaptured(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements PaymentEvent {} record PaymentRefunded(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Rejected {} record Ok(PaymentEvent event) implements Parsed {} record Rejected(String reason) implements Parsed {} static String field(Map<String, String> fields, String name) { String v = fields.get(name); if (v == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing field '" + name + "'"); return v; } static Money amount(Map<String, String> fields) { String raw = field(fields, "amountMinor"); try { return new Money(Long.parseLong(raw)); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("amountMinor is not a whole number: '" + raw + "'"); } } /** The edge: raw fields in, a model value or a reason out. It never throws. */ static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) { try { String type = field(fields, "type"); return switch (type) { case "captured" -> new Ok(new PaymentCaptured(new PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields))); case "refunded" -> new Ok(new PaymentRefunded(new PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields))); default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'"); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a constructor or a reader said no } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Map<String, String>> inbox = List.of( Map.of("type", "captured", "paymentId", "pay_7781", "amountMinor", "1999"), Map.of("type", "captured", "paymentId", "pay_7782", "amountMinor", "12.50"), Map.of("type", "refunded", "paymentId", "7781", "amountMinor", "500"), Map.of("type", "refunded", "paymentId", "pay_7781", "amountMinor", "-500"), Map.of("type", "captured", "paymentId", "pay_7783"), Map.of("type", "declined", "paymentId", "pay_7784", "reason", "CARD_EXPIRED")); int accepted = 0; for (Map<String, String> fields : inbox) { switch (parse(fields)) { case Ok ok -> { accepted++; System.out.println("OK " + ok.event()); } case Rejected r -> System.out.println("REJECTED " + r.reason()); } } System.out.println(accepted + " accepted, " + (inbox.size() - accepted) + " rejected"); } }

try.expect: One message passes and five are rejected: amountMinor is not a whole number: '12.50', invalid payment id: '7781', amount must not be negative: -500, missing field 'amountMinor' and unknown event type: 'declined'. The id and the sign were refused by the constructors, not by the parser. With your declined branch the last line reads 2 accepted, 4 rejected.

analogy: Think of the mailroom of a bank. Every envelope is opened there, once. A clerk either fills in the right typed form (a transfer, a complaint, a change of address) and sends it to a desk, or returns the letter with a note saying what was missing. The desks behind the mailroom only ever see forms, so they never squint at handwriting. The analogy breaks at one point: a good clerk may guess what a messy letter meant. The edge function must never guess. A missing amount is a rejection, not a zero.
world: In a Quarkus service the edge is usually the Kafka consumer: the deserializer hands you the record's JSON, parseEvent turns it into a PaymentEvent, and a Rejected goes to a dead-letter topic with the reason in a header, so the consumer can commit and move on. Webhooks from a card issuer, rows read back from an Oracle outbox table and signals into a Temporal workflow are edges too: each gets one parse function and nothing past it handles raw fields. When the producer team adds a new event type, deploy the consumers first: an old consumer rejects the unknown type at its edge and keeps running.
mistake: The common mistake is an edge that throws. parseEvent uses !!, toLong() and require directly, so a malformed message escapes as NullPointerException or NumberFormatException. In a Kafka consumer that exception fails the same record on every retry, and the partition stalls behind it. People write it because the throwing version is shorter and the happy-path test passes. The fix is to catch IllegalArgumentException once, around the whole parse, and return Parsed.Rejected(e.message), so the caller decides where the bad message goes. Keep the checks themselves in the constructors.

compare.title: The event model in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Model.java (Java 21)
java.html: record PaymentId(String value) { PaymentId { if (!value.matches("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid payment id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Money(long minor) { Money { if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative: " + minor); } @Override public String toString() { return BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, 2).toPlainString(); } } sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement { PaymentId paymentId(); } record PaymentAuthorized(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements PaymentEvent { PaymentAuthorized { if (amount.minor() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("authorized amount must be positive: " + amount); } } record PaymentDeclined(PaymentId paymentId, DeclineReason reason) implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded { Money amount(); } record PaymentCaptured(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } record PaymentRefunded(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } static String summary(PaymentEvent e) { return switch (e) { // no default case PaymentAuthorized(var id, var amount) -> id + " authorized " + amount + " EUR"; case PaymentDeclined(var id, var reason) -> id + " declined: " + reason; case PaymentCaptured(var id, var amount) -> id + " captured " + amount + " EUR"; case PaymentRefunded(var id, var amount) -> id + " refunded " + amount + " EUR"; }; }

kotlin.title: Model.kt
kotlin.html: @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) { init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid payment id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}") } } @JvmInline value class Money(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "amount must not be negative: $minor" } } override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, 2).toPlainString() } sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: PaymentId } data class PaymentAuthorized(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val amount: Money) : PaymentEvent { init { require(amount.minor > 0) { "authorized amount must be positive: $amount" } } } data class PaymentDeclined(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val reason: DeclineReason) : PaymentEvent sealed interface MoneyMovement : PaymentEvent { val amount: Money } data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } fun summary(event: PaymentEvent): String = when (event) { // no else is PaymentAuthorized -> "${event.paymentId} authorized ${event.amount} EUR" is PaymentDeclined -> "${event.paymentId} declined: ${event.reason}" is PaymentCaptured -> "${event.paymentId} captured ${event.amount} EUR" is PaymentRefunded -> "${event.paymentId} refunded ${event.amount} EUR" }

compare.note: The shape is the same: sealed interfaces for the alternatives, final carriers for the leaves, validation in the constructor, and one exhaustive switch per operation. Three things differ. Kotlin's value classes compile to a String and a long wherever they're used as themselves, while Java's PaymentId and Money records are separate objects until value records arrive with Valhalla. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them within one file), while Kotlin requires them to share the package and module. And a data class's copy() runs init, so captured.copy(amount = Money.ZERO) throws; records have no copy. kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does, so Java code can switch exhaustively over this Kotlin model, which lesson 3 relies on.

worked.title: Add a new event type, end to end

steps.say: Chargebacks arrive: a cardholder disputes pay_7781, and the card scheme holds 19.99 until it's decided. First decide where the event goes. Money is held, not captured or refunded, so it is not a MoneyMovement. It's a direct subtype of PaymentEvent, with the same positive-amount rule as the others.

drill.title: Write the hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write the sealed hierarchy from memory: PaymentEvent, the sealed MoneyMovement and the four leaves (plain String ids and Long amounts are fine). Then write movesMoney(e) with no else, using one branch for MoneyMovement. Finally, add PaymentDisputed and say which of your functions must change.

answer.html: sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class PaymentAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent data class PaymentDeclined(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentEvent sealed interface MoneyMovement : PaymentEvent { val cents: Long } data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: String, override val cents: Long) : MoneyMovement data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: String, override val cents: Long) : MoneyMovement fun movesMoney(e: PaymentEvent): Boolean = when (e) { is MoneyMovement -> true is PaymentAuthorized, is PaymentDeclined -> false } // PaymentDisputed : PaymentEvent breaks movesMoney (add `is PaymentDisputed -> false`). // A when over MoneyMovement alone would still compile.

alt.html: sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement { String paymentId(); } record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} record PaymentDeclined(String paymentId, String reason) implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded { long cents(); } record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, long cents) implements MoneyMovement {} record PaymentRefunded(String paymentId, long cents) implements MoneyMovement {} static boolean movesMoney(PaymentEvent e) { return switch (e) { case MoneyMovement m -> true; case PaymentAuthorized a -> false; case PaymentDeclined d -> false; }; } // PaymentDisputed (added to permits) breaks movesMoney: add `case PaymentDisputed d -> false;`.

recap: Stringly typed handlers each parse and check for themselves, so a bad message fails deep inside one of them after others have already acted on it.

A sealed interface closes the list of event types. Kotlin subtypes share its package and module; Java names them in permits. A sealed middle level such as MoneyMovement lets one branch stand for its leaves.
Write every operation as a when or switch with no else, so a new event type becomes a compile error at each place that must handle it.
Value classes make ids and amounts their own types at no cost where they're used as themselves, and their init blocks make every instance valid. One field only, so Money here is euro cents.
Parse once, at the edge, into the model. Return Ok or Rejected, never throw, and let the constructors make the checks. Behind the edge, trust the types.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why handlers take a PaymentCaptured instead of the Kafka record's Map<String, String>: "the map has everything, and it's one less type to maintain." Explain what the sealed model and the edge buy you, using a bug you could get with the map.
explain.answer: With the map, every handler parses and validates for itself. A capture with amount "12.50" throws inside the ledger after the audit handler already logged it, and a typo like "capture" silently never matches. The model closes the list of event types, so a when without else lists every place that must change when a type is added. Value classes make a swapped id and amount a compile error, and their constructors make every instance valid. The edge parses each record once and returns Ok or Rejected, so a bad message goes to the dead-letter topic before any handler acts. Behind it, a handler that takes a PaymentCaptured knows it has a valid id and a positive amount. The extra types cost a few lines; they remove a whole class of 2 a.m. bugs.

deeper.html:
Three questions come up once a model like this is in production.

How do events evolve? Adding a field with a default is safe for consumers that parse at the edge: old messages lack the field and get the default. Renaming a type or a field is not. Keep the old name in the parser for as long as old messages can arrive, and map it to the new type there, so the model itself never carries the history. If you serialize the model with kotlinx.serialization, as Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization showed, pin each type's name with @SerialName for the same reason.

Should the edge return Either instead of a sealed Parsed? Either<String, PaymentEvent> from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus works, and composes with map and flatMap. A dedicated Parsed reads better at the call site (is Parsed.Rejected) and leaves room for a third case later, such as Ignored for event types a service deliberately doesn't handle. Kotlin's Result<T> is the wrong fit: its failure side is a Throwable, and a rejection is not an exception.

What about the database? Rows you read back are untrusted input too. A column holding 'captured' and a nullable amount_minor is a raw map with a schema, and a migration or a manual fix can break it. Read rows through the same kind of edge function, or reuse parseEvent by turning each row into its field map.

Java has one tool here that Kotlin lacks: since JDK 21 a pattern switch can take case null explicitly, while Kotlin rules out null at compile time by declaring the parameter non-nullable. Both end up with the same guarantee behind the edge.
